title: Professor Quilliam's Wobbly Paths
markdown:
In a greenhouse that smelled of sun-warmed soil and ripe berries, Professor Quilliam kept a private weather of leaves. Tomatoes hung so plump and crimson they seemed pleased with themselves. He was a fox whose fur suggested toasted gingerbread and whose mind, though bright, often blew about like dandelion fluff. By trade he was a potter. His paws could coax a rim from clay as if the clay had been hoping for the invitation. His deeper passion was planning. Tea, shy dormice, the angle of a shelf: everything, he believed, improved if you drew it first. His diagrams were famous among those who had to step over them — arrows, boxes, little sketches that looked like dances in a hurry.

Edie the badger was the sensible weight on the other end of the string. She untangled his blueprints the way she buffed pots: with patience and a slightly raised brow. “Quilliam,” she would say, polishing terracotta, “this scheme for Optimal Squirrel Deterrence involves a trampoline and a confused pigeon. Are we sure?”

One crisp autumn morning, the sort that asks for wool and chocolate, news arrived. Inspector Grumbles of the Guild of Exemplary Artisans was coming. The Guild kept the country’s standards of craft. Inspector Grumbles could spot a glaze fault from a field away and spoke with the finality of a dropped anvil. Quilliam’s heart performed a small trapped flutter. Here was a chance to show not only bowls and jugs, but the architecture of his thinking, mapped in unmatched colour.

“Edie!” He bounced; his tail blurred. “The Inspector is nigh. A flawless visit needs a flawless strategy. A flawless strategy,” he tapped his snout, “needs a diagram that sings.”

Edie, paws dusty with potting soil, sighed a badger-sized sigh. “Sometimes a pot is a pot. A visit is a visit. Must even tea come with a flowchart like a nervous spider?”

“That,” said Quilliam, already bounding for the shed, “is where genius blossoms.” He returned with a vast sheet, a box of chalks in sunset and sky, and a heroic gleam. “The Optimal Visitor Experience Pathway. He shall see us structured. Orderly. Impressive.”

The morning became chalk. Arrows thick as his tail. Circles like bubbles. Among them, Edie suspected, were flying squirrels in ambitious poses — a Quilliam signature. He labelled as if writing scrolls: The Grand Welcome Nexus. The Artisan Showcase Quadrant. In pink, The Refreshment Interlude Sub-Protocol. He added a key in three colours, then a key to the key, then a small pot in the corner because a diagram without a pot felt unfurnished. At the journey’s end he sketched a surprisingly cheerful Inspector Grumbles giving an enormous thumbs-up.

Edie watched the paper grow until it threatened the tomato’s personal space. She moved a tray of drying bowls out of the traffic line and said nothing, which was one of her more advanced skills.

He propped the finished labyrinth against a towering tomato by the door, where no guest could miss it. Dusting imaginary specks from his paws, he declared it utterly perfect. “Now — tomatoes optimally arranged, if you please. Height, then hue, then, if we have time, philosophical ripeness.”

A stern badger arrived, fur creased with a general disappointment in the world. Inspector Grumbles surveyed the riot of fruit, then the diagram.

“Hmph.” Pebbles in a tin. “What is this edifice?”

Quilliam puffed. “The Optimal Visitor Experience Pathway. Your precise journey through my humble house. Method. Vision.”

The Inspector blinked from the colourful maze to the rows of plants. A bold red arrow ran past a cluster of fine beefsteaks and then snapped toward the potting bench.

“So this prominent line,” he said, claw precise, “means I proceed toward that exceedingly red tomato?”

“Precisely! The Primary Visual Inducement. Nature’s best, at once.”

Inspector Grumbles preferred directness to interpretation. He followed the red arrow to the beefsteaks as a map-reader follows a road. He stopped. He inspected. He made a note that might have been a score or a shopping list. The next mark, a wiggly blue, seemed to invite a meander through smaller, less ripe cherries. He took it at its word and began to weave, sniffing each plant with grave concentration, his shoulders brushing leaves, his dignity acquiring a faint green smear.

“And this sinuous path,” he muttered, “a thorough olfactory appraisal? An aromatic survey?”

Quilliam’s smile wavered. He had not, in his chalkiest dreams, meant the Inspector to get lost among cherries. He had meant him to admire the idea of a path, the beauty of a planned journey, not to treat every squiggle as treasure. A watering can stood where the pink protocol claimed a tasting stool should be. The Inspector politely sniffed the can, then looked at Quilliam as if awaiting the next official station. The structured light in Quilliam’s head flickered. The Guild was unfond of muddle. Pots, and a living, depended on a good report. He pictured a letter with a black stamp. He pictured Edie packing glaze. He did not, for a long breath, picture a way out that was not another arrow.

Edie stepped in as if she had been waiting for the muddle to ripen. She picked a deep-red tomato, skin bright, and held it out. “Perhaps, sir,” she said, still as a pond, “the diagram is less a strict map than a promise. Of things worth finding, if one takes time.”

The Inspector accepted the fruit. His brow stayed a landscape of furrows. He looked again at the cheerful mess, at the little drawn Grumbles still offering that thumbs-up. A hint of dawn touched his mouth.

“A promise.” He bit. The skin popped. Juice of summer and earth. A sweet smell rose. “Well, Mr. Quilliam, if this chaotic picture leads to produce like this, perhaps your Optimal Experience is not only rigid order.” He gestured with the dripping fruit. “The serpentine path found me cherries I would have marched past. They are quite… promising.”

Quilliam caught Edie’s glance and let the old explanation die. He would not rescue the arrows. He would keep the bite.

“Indeed!” His absent mind turned, for once, into charm. “Suggestions. Whispers of direction. A potter’s planning: you find your own way to a good pot, and to a good tomato.”

Inspector Grumbles chuckled, pebbles become musical. “Unique. I will grant you that. The results,” a wave at the abundant rows, “are excellent.” He looked at Edie with actual warmth. “And your friend knows how to present a good thing, planned or found. Practicality makes the brilliance edible.”

When he left, he carried a basket of the house’s best — beefsteaks, a handful of the overlooked cherries, and a small bowl Edie slipped in without ceremony — a hearty word for the pottery, and a new softness toward paths that wiggled. He paused at the door, glanced once more at the thumbs-up drawing, and gave the paper a nod that was almost a colleague’s.

Quilliam watched the stern back grow smaller among the hills. He did not announce a theory of joy. He only picked up a pot Edie had set to dry, turned it in his paws, and, when a drip of tomato found the rim, left the drip where it was. Edie returned to buffing, the quiet music of cloth on clay. The glass above them held the last of the autumn sun. Between the beefsteaks and the cherries the chalk arrows still pointed, and for the first time he did not mind if someone followed the blue one and got happily lost.
characters: Professor Quilliam (absent-minded fox potter), Edie (badger friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
